source.title: Training Load and Injury Part 2: Questionable Research Practices Hijack the Truth and Mislead Well-Intentioned Clinicians

paper.citation: Impellizzeri F.M., Ward P., Coutts A.J., Bornn L., McCall A. Training Load and Injury Part 2: Questionable Research Practices Hijack the Truth and Mislead Well-Intentioned Clinicians. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2020;50(10):577-584. doi:10.2519/jospt.2020.9211.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Is the methodological rigor of training-load and injury studies sufficient to support clinical decisions about modifying training for injury reduction? Participants: No new participant sample; this is a clinical and methodological commentary. Sport and level: Training-load and injury research across sport. Design: Clinical commentary and methodological critique. Exposure or intervention: Not applicable.
paper.tldr: The authors argue that absent conceptual and causal frameworks plus unreliable methods create conditions for selective reporting and confirmation bias. They conclude that evidence-based practical load-injury applications cannot currently be identified with confidence from the available research. Keep monitoring load because exposure matters operationally, but separate description, prediction, and causation.
paper.methods: Design: Clinical commentary and methodological critique. Exposure or intervention: Not applicable. Comparator: Not applicable. Measurements and outcomes: Conceptual clarity, causal structure, researcher degrees of freedom, selective reporting, and clinical claims. Analysis: Examples and reasoning about bias, P hacking, hypothesizing after results, and confirmation bias.
paper.findings: The authors argue that absent conceptual and causal frameworks plus unreliable methods create conditions for selective reporting and confirmation bias. They conclude that evidence-based practical load-injury applications cannot currently be identified with confidence from the available research. Their strongest practical statement is the generic principle not to do too much too soon, explicitly presented as accepted training practice rather than a finding confirmed by the reviewed studies.
paper.limitations: This is an expert critique, not an empirical estimate of the size of bias or a test of a replacement monitoring model. Interpretation: The paper challenges unsupported causal and prescriptive claims; it does not argue that training load is irrelevant or should not be monitored.
paper.practicalImplications: Keep monitoring load because exposure matters operationally, but separate description, prediction, and causation. Predefine questions where possible, retain continuous data, avoid post-hoc threshold shopping, show uncertainty, and resist converting associations into injury-prevention guarantees. Contextual coaching judgment remains necessary, but should be labeled as judgment.
